Before Teotihuacan became a city (c. 100 BCE) the Basin of Mexico held farming villages and the rival centre of Cuicuilco

Teotihuacan founded c. 100 BCE, dominant in the Basin of Mexico; its ruling-class centre was burned c. 550 and the state fell. Its reach beyond the Basin was largely prestige and trade, so Puebla, the Bajío and Michoacán are not coloured
Xochicalco, Epiclassic city-state in Morelos founded c. 650, burned and abandoned c. 900
Tula (Hidalgo) at its height c. 900-1150 ruled a regional state covering most of Hidalgo and the Valley of Mexico
After Tula's fall Chichimec groups moved into the Basin of Mexico, before the Tepanec state took shape

The Tepanec state of Azcapotzalco took shape 1200-1230 and under Tezozomoc (1367-1427) ruled most of the Valley of Mexico until the Triple Alliance destroyed it in 1428. The map gave the Basin to a 'Mixtec Empire' from 1280 and to Matlatzinca 1400-1428
Culhuacan, the Toltec successor city in the southern Basin, kept its prestige after Tula's fall; the Mexica settled as its vassals (1299) before founding Tenochtitlan
Tenochtitlan founded c. 1325 on Tepanec land, paying tribute and military service to Azcapotzalco until 1428; this province holds the island city
After Tula's fall Hidalgo was Otomi country until the lordship of Metztitlan
Cholula, a city from at least the 2nd century BCE: Olmeca-Xicallanca capital c. 700-1200, then Tolteca-Chichimeca; the map gave it to the Zapotecs, Monte Albán and Tenochtitlan
Monte Albán never ruled Puebla; before Cholula grew into a city (2nd century BCE) the Puebla valley held farming villages
Cantona, a fortified city of up to 80,000 controlling the eastern Puebla basin routes: first peak 50-600, apogee 600-1000, abandoned after 1050. The map gave the area to Toltec Tula
El Tajín, a centralised city-state that controlled much of Veracruz, flourished 600-1200 and was burned in the early 13th century
After El Tajín fell the north Veracruz coast was Huastec country (Huaxtec chiefdoms from 1400)
Olmec heartland of southern Veracruz and Tabasco, c. 1500-400 BCE (San Lorenzo, then La Venta); a culture without an attested state

Epi-Olmec culture centred on Tres Zapotes after La Venta's abandonment
Before Monte Albán the Valley of Oaxaca held Zapotec chiefdoms (San José Mogote); it was not Olmec land

Monte Albán, founded c. 500 BCE, capital of an expansionist Zapotec state by 100 BCE-200 CE; lost pre-eminence by the end of the Late Classic and was largely abandoned by 900-1000. One name (the map also used 'Zapotec Civilization' and 'Zapotec Empire')
Monte Albán conquered or colonised the Ejutla and Sola de Vega valleys south of the Valley of Oaxaca
After Monte Albán the Valley of Oaxaca split into dozens of competing Zapotec polities
Zaachila, the last Zapotec capital after Monte Albán, flourished c. 1100-1521 (name as used from 1400)
Southern Zapotec valleys after Monte Albán's decline
Zaachila's Zapotec kingdom in the southern valleys (name as used from 1400)
Mixteca Alta: Mixtec city-states (Yucuita, Monte Negro, later Tilantongo's first dynasty)
Eight Deer Jaguar Claw took Tilantongo in 1098 and made it the leading Mixtec kingdom of the Mixteca Alta
Oaxaca coast (Mixtec and Chatino) before Tututepec
Mixtec kingdom of Tututepec founded by Eight Deer in 1083 on the Oaxaca coast (influence over 25,000 km2 by contact); conquered by the Spanish in 1522
Isthmus of Tehuantepec: Mixe, Zoque and Huave country; not Olmec, Monte Albán or a Zapotec empire before the 15th century
Tarascan state founded c. 1300 by Tariácuri around Lake Pátzcuaro (Pátzcuaro, Ihuatzio, Tzintzuntzan); the map gave the lake to a 'Mixtec Empire' 1280-1400
By c. 1350 Tariácuri's lineage held all the Pátzcuaro centres and Hiripan extended expansion toward Lake Cuitzeo
Postclassic Guanajuato was Chichimec country (Guamare, Pame), not a Mixtec empire

El Mirador, capital of the Mirador Basin, peaked from the 3rd century BCE (possibly the earliest Maya state) and was abandoned c. 150 CE
Tikal (Mutal): dynasty founded perhaps in the 1st century, Classic peak c. 200-900, last monument 869
Naranjo (Saal), first known king 546, defeated by Tikal 744, abandoned c. 810
Calakmul: a royal seat from at least 411; seat of the Kaan (Snake) dynasty from the 630s and Tikal's great rival; last monument 909
Palenque, capital of Bʼaakal, kings from 431 to the accession of Janaab Pakal III in 799; no elite building after c. 800
Yaxchilan, dynasty from 359, apogee under Itzamnaaj Bʼalam II and Bird Jaguar IV, last monument 808
Caracol, dynasty founded 331, golden age under Kʼan II (618-658), last monument 859, core abandoned c. 900
Copán refounded as a kingdom's capital by Kʼinich Yax Kʼukʼ Moʼ in 426; last king Ukit Took acceded 822, collapse c. 800-830
Quiriguá's dynasty began in 426 as a vassal of Copán controlling the Motagua route
Kʼakʼ Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quiriguá captured and executed Copán's king in 738 and ruled independently; last texts 810
Kaminaljuyu, the leading highland Maya centre of the Late Preclassic (apogee c. 400-100 BCE), controlling the obsidian and jade routes
Chichen Itza rose c. 750-900 and as a regional capital (900-1050) controlled north and central Yucatán with tribute from conquered cities; declined by 1100
